name: Payeeproof — audit-ready payee change verification for public finance offices
one_liner: For the business manager of a small school district, town or county, Payeeproof is the one place every vendor bank-change and employee direct-deposit-change request lands: it pulls the known-good contact from the payee file, places and records an AI-assisted verification callback, forces a second approver, and emits a one-page, tamper-evident evidence PDF the state auditor and the cyber insurer will accept.
problem: Public finance offices change where money goes based on an email. A vendor (or someone who has taken over the vendor's mailbox) emails "we've switched banks, here's a new ACH form." An employee submits a direct-deposit change through self-service. Today, in districts and towns with a 2-6 person business office, the AP clerk is supposed to call a known-good number, get a second approver and write it down. Florida Auditor General operational audits repeatedly find this did not happen: in one district, no record of independent verification for 54 address changes and 8 of 10 bank-account changes; another audit cites $359,566 of electronic payments sent to an incorrect account and recommends a vendor-change log; others (Orange, Charlotte, Okeechobee counties) recommend documented direct contact with designated vendor staff plus independent review. Losses are real and recurring: Mansfield City Schools ~$54k (2025), Texarkana AR district nearly $2M diverted with $204,890 unrecovered, Sudbury (MA) schools $12,825 of payroll diverted after four employee direct-deposit changes were approved without independent confirmation, and City of Mobile's reported $14.7M. The control fails not because people don't know the rule, but because the "rule" lives in a Word SOP, the call happens on someone's mobile, and nothing is captured — so there is no evidence for the auditor, and TASB warns that failure to independently authenticate third-party payment instructions can jeopardise cyber coverage.
target_customer: Buyer: the director of business services / finance director / comptroller of a US K-12 district (1,000–15,000 students) or a town/county under ~100,000 population; secondary buyer, the controller of a 20–150 person nonprofit or clinic group. Users: 1-3 AP and payroll clerks. These are the organisations that sit below PaymentWorks' and Trustpair's enterprise onboarding programs but still get operationally audited every three years (Florida requires it by statute) and still move millions by ACH. ~13,300 regular public school districts and ~19,500 municipalities in the US (NCES/Census).
why_now: Three things landed in 2026. (1) Nacha's risk-management rules: Phase 1 hit all ODFIs and large originators on 20 March 2026 and Phase 2 hit every remaining non-consumer originator on 22 June 2026 — every organisation sending ACH now needs documented, risk-based processes to catch entries "authorized under false pretenses," reviewed annually. It mandates a documented process, not a product, which is exactly the shape of a cheap evidence tool. (2) Cyber/crime policies increasingly make independent authentication a condition; 2026 coverage litigation (Interstate Removal, a title-company bond case requiring a callback to a predetermined number plus a contemporaneous record) turned on whether the insured could show the step happened. (3) The callback itself is now automatable: outbound voice agents run at ~$0.07–$0.31/min (Vapi, Retell, Bland, ElevenLabs), and small typed-output decision models shipped this week (Liquid LFM3 d1, Parallel Decisions API at $0.001/request) make "does this request match the payee record and does the web still support this entity" a cheap, citable check rather than a research project.
comparables: PaymentWorks (paymentworks.com) — vendor identity and onboarding platform, strong in state/local government and higher ed (Seminole County FL, Frederick County Public Schools, State of Idaho); quote-only, and the core motion is inviting every vendor to self-register in a portal. Gap: a 2,500-student district will not re-onboard 800 vendors; it just needs the ~5-20 change requests a month handled and evidenced. Trustpair (trustpair.com) — enterprise third-party fraud prevention, custom pricing with annual evaluation volumes; reviewers describe it as suited to companies with thousands of vendors. Gap: too big, too expensive, no public SMB tier. Eftsure — payee verification with audit logs, quote-only, mid-to-large focus; does not appear to place the call. nsKnox PaymentKnox — publishes SMB pricing at $800/mo (Essentials) / $1,200/mo (Essentials Plus with automated callback support) and markets an "AI Agent Caller" that schedules, records and summarises verification calls; this is the closest competitor to the wedge, but it is a payments-security vendor selling to corporate treasury, not to a district business manager, and the price is ~3x what a small district will approve without a board item. CallbackProof (callbackproof.com) — $99–$199/mo hash-chained callback log for bookkeeping firms managing client AP; proves the evidence-record format sells, but targets accounting firms and does not place calls or cover payroll direct-deposit changes. BankChangeGuard — $99/mo, QuickBooks Online only, email one-time-code rather than a phone callback. Open gap: nobody is selling a cheap, payroll-plus-vendor change desk, pre-loaded with the audit language state auditors use, to the public-sector business office that gets the finding.
market_note: Estimate, clearly labelled: ~13,300 school districts + ~19,500 municipalities + tens of thousands of counties, authorities and mid-size nonprofits. If 5% of districts and municipalities buy at $3,000–$6,000/year (a price band consistent with small business-office tools, though I found no published benchmark), that is roughly $5–10M ARR at 5% penetration and a credible $50M+ category if nonprofits, clinics and bookkeeping firms are included. Willingness to pay is anchored not on ROI maths but on two things buyers already fund: avoiding a repeat audit finding, and keeping cyber coverage. Comparable published prices: nsKnox PaymentKnox Essentials $800/month (100 validations), CallbackProof $99–$199/month for bookkeeping firms, BankChangeGuard $99/month for one QuickBooks company. Trustpair, PaymentWorks, Eftsure and apexanalytix are all quote-only and enterprise-shaped.
risks: 1. Budget reality in small public bodies. Districts may treat this as a policy problem solved by a free SOP template, and procurement cycles are slow and seasonal (budgets set in spring for a July fiscal year). The $800/mo nsKnox tier existing does not prove a $300/mo tier sells to a district. 2. The callback is only as good as the known-good contact. If the phone number on file was never verified, or the vendor's AP line is an IVR that an AI agent cannot navigate, the product produces confident evidence of a worthless check — a liability, not an asset. Recording consent in all-party-consent states (CA, FL, MD, WA) adds friction and must be handled in the opening line. 3. Incumbent squeeze from below and above: nsKnox's AI Agent Caller already exists, CallbackProof already owns the "evidence PDF" idea for firms, and an ERP vendor (Tyler, Skyward, Blackbaud) could ship a change-verification workflow as a checkbox feature.
riskiest_assumptions: 1. A school district or town business manager will sign a $3-6k/year purchase order for this rather than writing a one-page SOP, and will do so outside the annual budget cycle. Most fragile: I found audit findings and losses, but zero published evidence of small-district software budgets or price points for this category. 2. The AI-assisted callback actually completes against real small-vendor phone numbers at a useful rate (reaching a named person at a number already on file, not voicemail or an IVR), and recording consent does not kill it. Untested. 3. Auditors and cyber underwriters will accept the generated evidence pack as satisfying "independent verification, documented" — i.e. the artefact is the thing that closes the finding. TASB and the Florida AG language supports the requirement; nobody has told me their PDF would count.
first_customers: Ten named, reachable places: (1) the Florida districts that received 2025–2027 operational audit findings on vendor information changes — Orange, Charlotte and Okeechobee county school districts are named in published AG reports, and every Florida district is audited at least every three years under s.11.45, so the finding list is a public prospect list; (2) districts with a public loss — Mansfield City Schools (OH), Texarkana AR SD, Sudbury Public Schools (MA); (3) state association and risk-pool channels: TASB Risk Management Fund (its own guidance says failure to independently authenticate may jeopardise coverage), state ASBO chapters, state GFOA chapters (GFOA publishes a bank-account-fraud-prevention best practice), and NJSBA/CASB co-op purchasing contracts; (4) regional CPA firms that run single audits for 20+ districts and keep writing the same management letter comment. Go where the finding was just issued: a business manager who has a draft audit comment in hand has a deadline and a board meeting.
validation_test: This week: pull 15 published state-auditor reports (Florida AG, Washington SAO, Ohio AoS) that contain a vendor-information-change or direct-deposit finding from the last 18 months, and email each named business manager or finance director a one-page PDF: their own finding language on the left, a mocked Payeeproof evidence pack for that exact finding on the right, and the line "we'll set this up for your next change request for $250/month, cancel anytime." Pass = 3+ replies and 2+ calls booked within 10 days, with at least one asking about purchase-order mechanics or co-op contract availability. Fail = polite "we've updated our procedures" replies with no meeting. Second, cheaper test in parallel: buy 50 outbound minutes on Vapi or Retell and run an AI callback script against 20 real small-business AP lines pulled from a public vendor list; pass = 60%+ reach a human who can confirm or deny a detail. That one test retires the biggest technical risk for under $50.
build_plan: Stack: TypeScript + Next.js, Postgres, a hosted voice agent (Vapi or Retell) for the outbound call, Whisper/provider transcription, a small typed-output model (Liquid LFM3 d1 or any structured-output call) to turn the transcript into {confirmed | denied | unreachable | suspicious} with the quoted lines, and server-side hash-chained append-only logging. No ERP integration in v1 — the fit with the builder's UiPath background is that Munis/Skyward/Blackbaud write-back is a later RPA job, not a v1 dependency. Steps: (1) Change intake: a forwarding address (changes@district.payeeproof.com) plus a public web form the district links from its vendor page; the request is parsed into payee, old/new bank, requester, channel. (2) Known-good contact: the district uploads a vendor/employee contact CSV once; the product shows the contact on file and explicitly refuses to use any number from the request. (3) Callback: one click places the recorded, consent-disclosed AI call to the on-file number, asks three scripted questions, and attaches transcript + recording + outcome. Human can place the call instead and dictate the result — the evidence pack must work either way. (4) Second approver: email link, named person, timestamped. (5) Evidence pack: one-page PDF with who requested, which on-file contact confirmed, how and when, who approved, hash chain, plus a short "procedure" appendix written in the language of Nacha Phase 2 and state-auditor findings. Cut from v1: ERP write-back, bank-account ownership validation (partner or skip — be clear it is a process control, not an ownership check), payment execution, multi-entity, SSO, mobile app.
launch_post:
A school district lost $54k because someone emailed "we changed banks."

Payeeproof is the one inbox every vendor bank change and payroll direct-deposit change goes to. It calls the number already on file, records it, forces a second approver, and hands you the one-page PDF your auditor asks for.
reasoning: Payeeproof won because it was the only candidate where I could find, in public documents, the buyer, the failure, the dollar amount and the exact missing artefact in the same place. State auditors are writing the sales pitch: Florida AG reports name districts with no record of independent verification for 54 address changes and 8 of 10 bank changes, and recommend documenting "who requested, verified, authorized and entered" each change — which is literally the product's output PDF. Losses are concrete and recent (Mansfield $54k, Texarkana ~$2M with $204,890 unrecovered, Sudbury $12.8k in payroll diversion, Mobile $14.7M reported). Nacha Phase 2 on 22 June 2026 made documented risk-based processes an obligation for every non-consumer ACH originator, and TASB's risk pool warns that failing to independently authenticate payment instructions can jeopardise cyber coverage — so there are three separate people who can force the purchase. It does not repeat anything in the library: Receipts files evidence of payer-portal submissions for medical billers, Holdroom supervises live AI phone calls for ops teams, and Mandate approves outbound insurance-agency messages. Payeeproof's buyer is a public-sector business manager and its workflow is inbound payee-change verification, a different event entirely; the AI callback is one step inside it rather than the product. It also fits the builder: a forwarding inbox, a hosted voice agent, a typed-output model and a PDF generator is a two-to-four-week v1 in TypeScript, and the ERP write-back later is exactly UiPath work. What keeps it off an 8: I could not find a single published price paid by a small district for a tool like this, and I could not confirm the AI callback connects at a useful rate against small-vendor phone lines. Those are the two things to test this week, and both are cheap.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Skill-diet-as-a-service / agent context budget monitor for platform teams (from @nicopreme) — dropped at generate: too close to past ideas Shelf and Skillscope, same buyer (agent builders), and the free OSS skill already does it. 2. Agent tool-call approval gateway for non-engineering teams (from @digitalocean Action Gateway) — dropped at generate: this is Holdroom in the library, and DigitalOcean/NVIDIA are now shipping it natively. 3. On-device multimodal inspection agent for field trades using LFM3-VL (from @liquidai) — dropped at screen: real buyer (insurance/utility field inspectors) but needs hardware, long sales cycle, and 3+ months before a first sale; wrong fit for evenings and weekends. 4. Web-grounded lead/customer record refresher built on the Parallel Decisions API (from @p0) — dropped at screen: Fiber AI, Clay and a dozen enrichment vendors already sell exactly this to exactly this buyer; crowded and the API is a commodity anyone can call. 5. Supplier master-data hygiene agent for procurement (stale banking, duplicates, dead vendors) — finalist, but merged into the pick: data-quality framing has no urgency and competes with Ivalua/apexanalytix; the change-request moment is where the money and the deadline are. 6. HTS/tariff reclassification watcher for small importers — dropped at screen: 2026 is thick with trade-compliance vendors (Gaia Dynamics, Quickcode, bitedata) chasing the same tariff churn, and the builder has no customs domain access. 7. Carrier appetite-change tracker for independent insurance agencies — dropped at screen: adjacent to the library's Mandate (same buyer), and First Connect and the MGA platforms already aggregate appetite. 8. Grant-condition change monitor for nonprofit grants managers — dropped at screen: real latent pain, but Instrumentl and Thompson Grants occupy the space, budgets are thin and the compliance event is annual, not weekly. 9. Periodic KYB/CDD refresh desk for credit unions and small banks — dropped at screen: heavily funded incumbents (Alloy, Sardine, Abrigo across 2,500 institutions) and a 9-month regulated sales cycle. 10. Payeeproof: payee-change verification and evidence desk for small public finance offices — PICK. Named buyer, recurring weekly event, a June 2026 compliance deadline, published audit findings naming the exact missing artefact, and the incumbents are all enterprise-priced portals.

PROJECT
1. Expiry — URL in, per-claim freshness card with a Still True score + weekly re-check. PICK: new API makes it newly cheap, personal (your own post), output is a number people post, weekly reason to return.
2. Oracle — paste any "will X happen" question, get a web-grounded probability card. Finalist, lost: Oracle Markets, OddsShopper and OrcaLayer already publish AI-vs-market probability dashboards with Brier scores; crowded and the output is a number with no personal stake.
3. Drift Board — AI's probability vs Polymarket odds, biggest disagreements daily. Dropped at screen: github shows many LLM-vs-market tools (homerun, polymarket-agents, OctagonAI kalshi bot) and oraclemarkets.io does exactly this.
4. SkillSlim web — paste a SKILL.md, see what a diet would cut. Dropped: thin clone of nicopreme's skill-diet, and too close to past ideas Shelf/Skillscope.
5. Lens — LFM3-VL-2B running on-device, webcam in, spatial description out. Finalist, lost: browser deployment unconfirmed (ONNX export exists but no verified in-browser runtime), so buildability risk over a weekend is real.
6. EarCheck — LFM3-Audio-2B turns a voice memo into typed decisions. Dropped at screen: needs local GPU/laptop setup, not a link anyone can click.
7. Hetzner Bill — paste your AWS bill, see the bare-metal equivalent (from @SimonHoiberg's $8k→$300). Dropped: needs bill parsing plus made-up equivalence; a calculator, nothing to share twice.
8. Gate — paste an agent's tool-call log, get an allow/deny/ask policy card (from the DigitalOcean Action Gateway post). Dropped: audience too small, output not shareable, and overlaps past idea Proofline/Holdroom territory.
9. RWE Cards — turn the RWE-Bench physical-engineering tasks into a browsable card wall. Dropped at screen: dataset contents and licence unverified, and it is a gallery with no personal input.
10. Mode — a browsable wall of the focus "modes" people build for AI docks (from @trq212). Dropped: no public dataset exists, would have to be invented.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3 of 3): Parallel Decisions API (confirmed $0.001/request, web-grounded typed decisions, explicitly pitched at "refresh stale banking records" — which seeded the payee-data angle), DigitalOcean Action Gateway (confirmed it is a shipped allow/deny/ask tool-policy layer, which killed candidate 2 as a repeat of Holdroom against a now-native feature), Liquid LFM3 / d1 decision models (typed outputs and calibrated probabilities on 2B open-weight models, fine-tunable on one GPU — the cheap classifier layer in the build plan). I also spent one extra summary on skill-diet, which confirmed candidate 1 was a solved OSS problem.

Screening pot (6 of 6): one search each on eligibility-rule monitoring, supplier master data, KYB refresh, carrier appetite, grant compliance and HTS/tariff. Four died here on crowding or sales-cycle length. The supplier master-data search was the one that paid off — it surfaced "stale banking details" and vendor-change fraud as the live, named pain inside an otherwise boring data-quality category, which redirected the whole night.

Deep research pot (12 of 12): mapped the competitive floor and ceiling (Trustpair/PaymentWorks/Eftsure/apexanalytix all quote-only and enterprise-shaped; nsKnox Essentials at $800/mo with an AI Agent Caller; CallbackProof at $99–$199/mo for bookkeeping firms; BankChangeGuard at $99/mo for QBO), established the regulatory clock (Nacha Phase 1 20 Mar 2026, Phase 2 22 Jun 2026, risk-based and documentation-shaped with no prescribed product), gathered the loss and audit evidence (Mansfield $54k, Texarkana ~$2M / $204,890 unrecovered, Sudbury $12,825 payroll, Broward 40 unreviewed change requests, Mobile $14.7M reported, Florida AG findings naming Orange/Charlotte/Okeechobee, Washington SAO on Mercer Island, a Florida report citing $359,566 misdirected), checked the insurance angle (2026 coverage disputes turning on documented callbacks; TASB RMF tying independent authentication to coverage), sized the buyer universe (~13,300 districts, ~19,500 municipalities), and priced the callback technology (Vapi/Retell/Bland/ElevenLabs ~$0.07–$0.31/min, plus all-party-consent recording constraints). Two searches returned nothing usable (Reddit AP complaints, nonprofit finance directors) — that absence is why market_pull is capped at 7: I have audit evidence, not purchase evidence.

Sharpening pot (2 of 5): one call confirmed Florida's vendor-change findings are a recurring statutory audit objective rather than a one-off, and one confirmed employee direct-deposit changes are a separately audited, separately lossy failure mode worth folding into the same desk. Three sharpening calls unspent because the two changes both survived first contact and further calls were unlikely to move a score I could defend; the remaining unknowns (district price points, callback connect rates) need primary contact, not search — which is what the validation test does this week.
Sharpening (7 to 7.6): Round 1 — weakest criterion: gap (6 before). The original candidate was a generic "AI vendor bank-change verification for mid-market finance teams." Research found that space is genuinely contested at the low end: nsKnox publishes an SMB tier at $800/mo and markets an AI Agent Caller that places, records and summarises verification calls; CallbackProof sells a $99–$199/mo hash-chained callback log; BankChangeGuard sells a $99/mo QuickBooks workflow. So I changed the idea: move the buyer from the generic mid-market controller to the small public finance office (K-12 district business manager, town comptroller), where the forcing function is not ROI but a recurring statutory operational audit. Evidence that held: Florida AG audits repeatedly cite exactly this control across multiple districts (Orange, Charlotte, Okeechobee, plus a report citing $359,566 misdirected and recommending a vendor-change log); Florida statute requires district operational audits at least every three years; Washington SAO made the same finding against the City of Mercer Island; TASB RMF ties independent authentication to coverage. None of the three cheap incumbents targets or integrates with this buyer — CallbackProof sells to bookkeeping firms, BankChangeGuard to QuickBooks companies, nsKnox to corporate treasury — and the enterprise players (PaymentWorks, Trustpair, Eftsure) sell portal onboarding at quote-only prices. gap 6 → 8; pain 7 → 8 on the named losses and findings.

Round 2 — weakest remaining: timing (7 before) and market_pull (7). Change to the idea: widen the change types from vendor bank details to all payee-detail changes including employee direct deposit, and anchor the evidence pack's wording on the Nacha Phase 2 obligation. Evidence found: Nacha Phase 2 bound every remaining non-consumer originator on 22 June 2026 to documented, annually reviewed, risk-based fraud processes — a documentation mandate, not a product mandate, which is precisely what a cheap evidence tool satisfies; and payroll diversion is an independently documented, separately audited failure (Sudbury Public Schools, $12,825 across two payrolls, changes approved with no independent confirmation; Minnesota OSA and NY Comptroller both publish direct-deposit verification guidance). That roughly doubles the number of change events per customer per month and gives the payroll director as a second internal champion. timing 7 → 8. market_pull stayed at 7: I confirmed the role, the obligation and the audit pressure, but found no published price any district actually pays for this category, so I will not score the budget line above 7 on inference. First score (average before sharpening) 7.0 → 7.6.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the Parallel Decisions API launch (confirmed $0.001/request, 100 questions per request, 5,000 free requests, 600 rpm, 200ms–1s), the LFM3 release (six ~2B models, LFM Open License v1.0, on HF with ONNX for VL, but NO confirmed in-browser deployment — this killed two candidates), and Decisions request/auth shape (x-api-key header, CORS unconfirmed → must use a serverless proxy, which set the build plan). Screening pot (5/5): searched prior art for pasted-claim fact-checkers, AI-probability forecast apps, landing-page claim scorers, Polymarket/Kalshi public APIs, and LLM-vs-market dashboards — the forecasting candidates died here (oraclemarkets.io, OddsShopper AI-vs-market scoreboard, several GitHub LLM-vs-odds tools). Deep research (8/8): confirmed no URL→README/claim freshness checker exists (closest: BCGen `skill-auditing` and bootgs `freshness-auditor` agent skills, SERP Delta with zero stars, HowToAI's paste-text hallucination checker); confirmed Parallel ToS permit public apps with per-visitor results but bar republishing stored output (so the Rot Board must be the builder's own small curated set, not a bulk dataset); confirmed Decisions supports choice/score types and returns response-level (not per-answer) citations — this changed the UI design so citations are shown as "what's true now" context, never as per-claim proof; confirmed Netlify free tier (125k invocations) covers launch. Sharpening pot (4/4): checked docs-rot leaderboards (DocsAlot, 215 sites, stale since June 2026), freshness/"still true" badges (only timestamp badges exist — Shields.io, cardd.cc), GitHub-Action docs-freshness tools (DocGuard checks commits-since-review, not web truth), and developer complaints about stale guidance. The weekly-watch and score-card changes survived; nothing well known does either.
Sharpening (7.8 to 8.4): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (7, a one-time "check my old post" toy). Change: added "Watch weekly" — save a URL, a daily cron re-checks it, and the page shows the Still True score over time plus "2 claims rotted this week"; plus a public Rot Board of ~30 well-known docs pages re-scored weekly so the site itself changes. Research: checked for prior art on docs-rot leaderboards and freshness badges — DocsAlot ranks 215 docs sites but site-level and last updated June 2026; Shields.io/cardd.cc badges only show a timestamp, never whether claims hold; no page-level weekly rot index found. Cost check: at $0.001 per Decisions request with 100 questions bundled, 200 watched pages re-checked daily is ~$6/month, inside the free $5 allowance at weekly cadence. Usefulness 7 → 8.
Round 2 — weak criterion: shareability (7, a list of verdicts is not a post). Change: the primary output became a card with one number on it (Still True 41/100) rendered as an OG image so the result link previews in a tweet, with the 3 reddest claims on it. Research: confirmed no existing tool produces a "% still true" card (closest are age-only freshness badges), so the number is novel and the self-own format ("my own tutorial scored 41") is the hook. Shareability 7 → 8. Wow stayed 8, not 9: the result is surprising but it is a verdict list, not something people screen-record.
prototype_summary: A clickable Payeeproof prototype showing a suspicious vendor bank-change email turning into a signed, auditor-ready evidence pack through a 4-step verification flow with fraud and legitimate scenarios.
